primary_link.title: LoomSC: Scalable Deep Subspace Clustering with Projector Factorization and Exact Spectral Reduction

papers.summary: Dense self-expression matrices and full-affinity spectral clustering limit the scalability of subspace clustering. We introduce the Latent Orthogonal Optimization Model for Subspace Clustering (LoomSC), a framework that addresses both bottlenecks through projector factorization and exact spectral reduction. Motivated by the spectral structure of least-squares regression, LoomSC jointly learns latent features and a projector self-representation through two thin factors. Alternating Procrustes and least-squares updates preserve the sample factor's orthogonality while keeping the coefficient matrix implicit. We construct a nonnegative quadratic affinity that preserves the projector's support. An exact feature map then reduces its normalized spectral problem to an eigenproblem whose dimension depends only on the factor width. Neither the full affinity nor the sample Laplacian needs to be formed. Our analysis quantifies the projector approximation and identifies conditions for subspace preservation and within-subspace connectivity. For fixed dimensions and iteration budgets, the complete pipeline has linear time and memory complexity in the number of samples. Across five image-clustering benchmarks, LoomSC ranks first or second in all 15 dataset-metric comparisons against 9 state-of-the-art baselines. Its mean accuracy exceeds the highest baseline mean by 6.66 percentage points. Synthetic experiments scale to 500,000 samples while maintaining at least 99.8% accuracy.
papers.summary_en: LoomSC addresses two scaling bottlenecks in subspace clustering: storing sample-to-sample self-expression coefficients and performing spectral decomposition on the full affinity matrix. It jointly trains an autoencoder and two thin factors, representing sample relationships implicitly through an orthogonal projector. Entrywise squaring produces a nonnegative affinity, and quadratic features transfer its spectral problem exactly to a space determined by the factor width. Read Algorithms 1 and 2 in Section III before Appendices B–D, distinguishing fixed-feature descent, clustering recovery under the full-row-space assumptions, and actual joint training: these have different guarantees. Across five image datasets, the method ranks first or second in all fifteen dataset–metric comparisons. Mean accuracy is about 80.17%, exceeding the best baseline mean by 6.66 percentage points; synthetic tests extend to 500,000 samples with reported accuracy of at least 99.8%. These results do not establish benefits for language or agent tasks. Linear time and memory claims require fixed dimensions, factor width and iteration budgets. The experimental width of 380 corresponds to a spectral feature dimension of 72,390, so asymptotic linearity alone does not show that small datasets become cheaper. When reading the speed figures in Table IV, ask whether timing includes both 5,000-epoch training phases and inspect hardware and solver settings. Missing width ablations, inconsistent initialization descriptions and incomplete reproduction details remain important checks before adoption.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.10253v1#page=4 — Proposition 1, Fig.1, pp.4–5, Equation 11: visiting smaller frontier a rather than b at the same length y strictly saves 2*y*(phi(a)-phi(b)); relabelled continuation and deletion of redundant sweeps cannot add cost.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.10253v1#page=9 — Main theorem: existence plus least-frontier and nondecreasing lengths permit least-recently-swept tie-breaking, giving a cyclic optimum for the specified distribution. This is not a proof that arbitrary input distributions have cyclic optima.

llm_evaluation.rationale: A focused and largely self-contained proof note closes a previously stated cyclic-reduction claim in randomized cow-path search. Its substantive contribution is online-algorithm theory, not language-model reasoning: the acknowledgment of AI assistance is not an evaluated method. Relevance to the preferred LLM/agent topics is consequently low, but the cow/robot metaphor does not make this a pure-robotics application subject to the enumerated scope cap. For a uniform choice of ray and a fixed power-law distance distribution, the proof combines least-frontier relabelling, a stationarity condition, deletion of insufficient advances, and an adjacent-sweep exchange to obtain nondecreasing lengths and cyclic tie-breaking. Importantly, Appendix A establishes existence of a minimizer using coordinatewise bounds and diagonal subsequences, rather than assuming an optimum. The core algebra, feasibility conditions, strict-improvement inequalities and compactness argument check out at the level of this review; exact arithmetic spot checks are corroboration, not formal verification. The result completes an old structural argument rather than improving the known competitive ratio or supplying a new practical search system. Its dependence on symmetric paths and the positive smooth power-law tail limits generalization; the truncated-distribution extension is explicitly left unresolved. Prior lower-bound papers and historical handwritten notes were not inspected, so historical priority and the complete earlier optimality theorem are not independently re-established. Both supplied appendices and all material equations/figures were read; no missing-source hold is needed.

primary_link.title: On the Cyclic Assumption of the Cow-Path Search Algorithm

papers.summary: In the cow-path problem, a cow must find a goal lying at an unknown distance on one of $w$ paths connected only at the origin, and performance is measured by competitive ratio. Kao, Reif and Tate designed an efficient randomized algorithm in which the cow visits the paths in a fixed cyclic order. They proved the algorithm is optimal for $w=2$, and subsequently Kao, Ma, Sipser and Yin proved its optimality for all $w$, with a claim that no algorithm does better than the best cyclic one. This note provides a detailed proof of that claim.
papers.summary_en: This proof note revisits an old cow-path search question. A target lies at an unknown distance on one of several paths sharing an origin, and a searcher makes out-and-back excursions. Can attention be restricted to a fixed cyclic order without sacrificing optimality? The authors supply a previously asserted but unpublished reduction proof; they do not improve the known competitive ratio. Start with Section 2 for the uniform choice of path, power-law distance distribution and remaining-weight function. Then follow Sections 3–6 through four steps: prioritize a path with the smallest frontier, use stationarity to identify insufficient advances that can be deleted, exchange adjacent sweeps to eliminate decreasing lengths, and break ties in favor of the least recently searched path to obtain a cycle. Do not skip Appendix A: it separately proves that an optimum exists rather than assuming that an infimum is attained. Figures 1 and 2 show how relabeling paths aligns the continuation states and are useful alongside the inequalities. The conclusion relies on symmetric paths and a positive, smooth power-law tail; it does not extend automatically to arbitrary target distributions. Section 7 explicitly leaves the truncated-distribution case open. The paper is useful for readers studying online algorithms and competitive analysis because it completes a structural proof. AI assistance mentioned in the acknowledgments is not an evaluated language-model reasoning method, and the paper contains no robot-deployment experiment.
papers.summary_zh: 這篇證明短文處理牛徑搜尋的一個老問題：目標位於共同原點延伸的多條路徑之一，位置未知，搜尋者來回探查，能否只考慮固定循環順序而不損失最佳性？作者補全先前只宣稱、未正式刊出的歸約證明，沒有改善既有競爭比。先讀第二節，掌握均勻選路、冪律距離分布與「剩餘權重」，再沿第三至六節追蹤四個步驟：優先搜尋前沿最小的路徑；由駐點條件找出可刪除的不足推進；交換相鄰掃描以排除長度下降；最後用最久未搜尋的路徑打破平手，形成循環。附錄Ａ不可略過，因為它另證明最佳解確實存在，避免把只有下確界的問題當成已有最小值。圖一、圖二說明重新標記路徑後如何對齊後續狀態，適合配合不等式閱讀。結論依賴對稱路徑及正、平滑的冪律尾部，不能直接推到任意目標分布；第七節明確保留截斷分布的疑問。本文適合研究線上演算法與競爭分析的讀者，價值在補齊結構性證明。致謝中的人工智慧協助並非經驗證的語言模型推理方法，也沒有機器人部署實驗。

primary_link.title: Active Inference for Interaction-Mediated Control of a High-Dimensional Robotic Arm

papers.summary: We propose interaction-mediated control via Active Inference as a general architectural approach to high-dimensional control problems in Human--Computer Interaction (HCI). This architecture recasts user interaction as the provision of evidence about a latent task objective, rather than the direct specification of plant-control inputs. The mediating function is distributed between an interaction broker, which selects informative user queries and performs Bayesian inference over user preferences, and an Active Inference controller, which autonomously plans and acts under the resulting preference information to control the plant. This division of labour decouples the semantics of user interaction from those of low-level plant control. We instantiate the architecture in a simulated, multi-link robotic arm to perform a simultaneous whole-arm target-coverage task. A simulated user communicates exclusively through a clutch-style binary evaluative channel, without specifying joint-torque commands. Across increasing arm dimensionalities, the architecture achieves successful interaction-mediated control, although task success is lower than when the controller receives the true target preferences directly. Exact target-subset identification also remains imperfect, highlighting the distinction between preference inference and successful task completion. The experimental findings provide an initial computational demonstration of the proposed architecture under controlled, matched-model assumptions and motivate its further investigation in broader HCI applications.
papers.summary_en: This paper separates low-bandwidth preference feedback from high-dimensional control. An interaction broker asks which previewed behaviors fit the user's objective, while a low-level controller independently plans and executes arm torques. The broker selects queries by expected information gain, receives a binary satisfaction response, and performs exact Bayesian updating over six possible target subsets. It sends object-wise target probabilities to the controller, rather than one most-likely target subset or a motor command. Read Section 3 and Figure 2 first: the queried trajectory is an information-gathering probe, and execution uses a freshly planned trajectory. Experiments use simulated arms with three to six links and four objects in one fixed layout; each episode requires simultaneous coverage of two targets. Across 576 episodes per condition, mediated control succeeds in 73.4%, versus 97.9% when the controller receives the true preferences directly. Exact target identification reaches only 16.7–47.2%, so task completion must be distinguished from correct intent inference, especially because touching non-targets is unpenalized. The user is simulated with a response-model family matching the broker's assumptions. Physics pauses during interaction, timing summaries include successful episodes only, and neither human response latency nor wall-clock computation is measured. No random-query or no-feedback comparison isolates the query policy's benefit. The useful contribution is an explicit interface between preference inference and autonomous control; robustness to real people, model mismatch and other tasks remains unestablished.

papers.summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) from outcome rewards suffers from sparse supervision, particularly on difficult, long-horizon tasks where successful trajectories are rare and costly to generate. On-Policy Distillation (OPD) offers an attractive alternative by providing dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher along the student's own generations. Self-distillation methods further remove the need for a separate teacher model by conditioning the same policy on privileged information to serve as its own teacher. However, privileged conditioning alone does not guarantee that the resulting distillation update improves the student. Indeed, privileged information can lead the teacher to solve tasks through shortcuts unavailable to the student, producing supervision poorly matched to the student's current behavior. Consequently, even a higher-performing teacher can provide guidance that degrades student performance. To address this, we analyze how the choice of privileged teacher affects the student's update. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the teacher's local distillation update to be a positive multiple of the student's reward gradient. Our analysis suggests that the teacher should not only perform well on the task, but also provide guidance suited to the student's current capabilities. This characterization motivates a practical teacher-training surrogate that combines outcome rewards with token-level Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the student. Based on this result, we propose Joint On-Policy Learning and Teaching (JOLT), which jointly trains a single policy in two roles: a privileged teacher using a KL-regularized objective, and an unprivileged student using dense on-policy distillation. Across mathematical reasoning, coding, tool use, and terminal use, JOLT improves training efficiency and performance, with further gains from student rewards.
papers.summary_en: A teacher that sees the answer need not teach well: privileged shortcuts can produce token-level guidance poorly aligned with the student's reward. JOLT trains one language model in two roles, a privileged teacher and an unprivileged student, each generating its own trajectories. The teacher learns from outcome rewards plus KL regularization toward the student; the student receives dense distillation on its own responses. JOLT+ adds student outcome rewards. The theory characterizes a local gradient for a fixed student, but the practical teacher substitutes its own returns, and shared-weight joint updates have no corresponding guarantee. Across three MATH training runs, mean accuracy rises from GRPO's 68.36% to 72.59% with JOLT+; JOLT reaches 72.14% without direct student reward. Teacher-objective ablations support practical value but cannot separate better teaching signals from direct transfer through shared weights. Coding accuracy of 49.08% versus 46.13% uses the same 131 training problems with additional unseen test cases, not unseen problems. Reported 13-fold completion-token and 6.5-fold processed-token savings compare an observed GRPO budget with a fitted JOLT budget at 63.44% MATH accuracy. These ratios lack confidence intervals and do not measure elapsed time. Gradient diagnostics use selected single training runs and noisy references. The complete 29-page paper is readable, but the full AppWorld scaffold and terminal shared prompt/tool schema remain unavailable in the reviewed packet. This assessment covers the method, mathematics and non-agent evidence, without endorsing agent-experiment reproducibility.

llm_evaluation.rationale: PHRBench's independently assessable value is separating compliance, avoidance and explicit correction from final-answer correctness. The 460 base questions, truthful/false contexts, 18 models and detailed tables permit a bounded evaluation of the benchmark design and author-reported descriptive trends. Table 1 yields a mean 7.7167-percentage-point decrease, but reconstruction from domain tables reveals different T/H domain weights, so it is not a pure matched-distribution contrast. More correction at larger scales within several families does not establish that scale causes either vulnerability or recovery. BUF is a thresholded KL statistic from a fixed Qwen2.5-7B reference distribution; correlations and selected examples do not identify the evaluated models' internal beliefs. The 95% behavioral-label audit lacks a sample size, and question-cluster uncertainty is unreported. The predictor's base-question split is a strength, but cross-model/repeated-response target aggregation, selection of 3,234 from 3,900 augmentations and the best-F1 selection set are unspecified. If precision .738 and recall .524 are pooled binary statistics at one threshold, F1 would be approximately .61286, not .531. Unknown averaging makes this an unresolved inconsistency, not proof of arithmetic error. Missing feature prompts, schemas, heuristic formulas and evaluation implementation prevent treating AUROC .847 as verified performance. These gaps do not erase the behavioral framework's value, but preclude stronger predictive, causal-mechanistic or real-agent generalization claims.

primary_link.title: PHRBench: A Behavioral Evaluation of Post-Hallucination Reasoning in LLMs

papers.summary: Hallucinated information can propagate through multi-stage LLM systems and become part of the context for subsequent reasoning. Existing studies of post-hallucination reasoning (PHR) mainly characterize changes in final outcomes and aggregate reasoning dynamics, leaving how models resolve hallucinated premises at the response level insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce PHRBench, a controlled benchmark for behaviorally structured PHR across four domains and 18 large language models. PHRBench characterizes each reasoning trajectory independently of final-answer correctness through Hallucination Compliance, Hallucination Avoidance, and Heuristic Correction, and defines an insightful trajectory as successful correction that ultimately reaches the correct answer. Across 4820 controlled instances, we find that successful recovery remains relatively rare and is associated with more frequent belief updates along the reasoning trajectory. We further find that properties of the hallucinated prompt contain substantial predictive signal for successful recovery, with a lightweight predictor achieving an AUROC of 0.847. These findings provide a behavioral view of post-hallucination reasoning, characterizing how LLMs resolve erroneous context and when successful recovery is likely to occur.
papers.summary_en:
A correct answer does not establish that a model recognized a false premise. PHRBench separates compliance, avoidance and explicit correction, defining successful recovery as correction followed by a correct answer. It selects 460 chemistry, biomedicine, physics and coding questions from eight existing benchmarks, adds 460 truthful and 3,900 hallucinated contexts, and evaluates the resulting 4,820 inputs on 18 models with ten samples per model–input pair. Its useful contribution is to distinguish answer correctness from how erroneous context is handled.

The reported mean accuracy loss is about 7.7 percentage points. Larger models within several families correct more often while also showing larger losses, but truthful and hallucinated conditions have different domain weights: this is not directly a matched-weight treatment effect. Nor are the 4,820 inputs independent questions. Belief Update Frequency measures distributional changes under a fixed Qwen2.5-7B reference scorer; it does not establish the evaluated model's internal beliefs or a causal correction mechanism.

A prompt-feature predictor reportedly reaches AUROC 0.847. Splitting by base question is a useful leakage safeguard, but the aggregation of prediction labels across models and repeated responses, the reduction from 3,900 augmentations to 3,234 prediction instances, and the selection and averaging conventions behind the best-F1 threshold are insufficiently specified. Exact feature prompts and formulas are also missing, preventing verification of predictive performance. The reported 95% manual label-audit accuracy lacks a sample size. The paper therefore supports a useful behavioral evaluation framework and bounded descriptive evidence, rather than a validated pre-deployment recovery predictor or demonstrated generalization to real agent systems.
papers.summary_zh:
答對問題，不代表模型已識破錯誤前提。PHRBench把回應區分為沿用幻覺、繞過幻覺及明確修正，另以「修正且答對」定義成功恢復。研究從八個既有基準選出460道化學、生醫、物理與程式題，加入460份真實敘述及3900份錯誤敘述，共4820個輸入；18個模型對每個輸入取樣十次。這個設計的價值，是把最終正確性與處理錯誤脈絡的行為分開，避免把碰巧答對誤認為可靠修正。

表中平均準確率下降約7.7個百分點；部分同家族較大模型雖更常修正，也更容易受錯誤脈絡影響。但真實與幻覺條件的領域權重不同，降幅不能直接當同權重配對效果；4820個輸入也非4820道獨立題目。所謂信念更新頻率，是固定Qwen2.5-7B評分器的分布變化，不能證明受測模型內部信念或修正的因果機制。

作者另報告提示特徵預測器AUROC為0.847，並按原題分割訓練與測試，這是有用的防洩漏設計。然而預測標籤如何跨模型與多次回應聚合、3900份增補縮為3234筆的規則、最佳F1閾值的選法與平均方式都不夠明確；精確特徵提示及公式亦缺失，故不能據此驗證預測效能。人工抽查95%標籤正確也未交代樣本量。這篇適合作為行為評估框架與受限的描述性證據，尚不足支持可靠的部署前恢復預測或真實代理系統泛化。

evidence: Sec. 3, pp. 3–5, Definitions 3.1–3.4/Fig. 1: graph-conditioned transition/reward families define CGMARL, with TS, CS and GFS subclasses. General RL methodology, not merely deployment of a fixed policy to robots.

Sec. 4 and App. C, pp. 5–6 and 18–20, Figs. 2/5: GRAFO uses topology and target shifts to define formation rewards; equivalent nodes receive targets by minimum-cost assignment. In this benchmark transitions remain those of the prior Formation environment.

Sec. 5.1, p. 6, Table 1: individual GRAFO-3/5 training reaches median solved fraction 1, but zero-shot transfer is 0 or 0.016; sequential unregularized training gives median 0 on the earlier task, with five seeds. This is one backbone on two tasks, not a universal impossibility result.

Sec. 5.2, pp. 6–7, Eqs. 4–5: FROG freezes the graph encoder after first-task learning and adapts the action module with existing continual-learning regularizers. It eliminates parameter-induced representation change at fixed inputs, not the action-module term.

App. A, p. 17, Eqs. 7–8, directly visually checked: the Lipschitz constant K^pi appears before triangle decomposition and is absent from both final summands. Eq. 5 inherits the omission; a negative signed return difference can satisfy the upper bound despite severe forgetting.

Sec. 6, pp. 7–9, Figs. 3–4: TS/CS/GFS contain 6/5/4 tasks and use 10 independent seeds; TS has 3–7 agents. Gains are broad but Fig. 3 TS EWC (O) has a lower AFP median with FROG. Figure 4 and text expose first-task and order dependence.

Sec. 6.2, p. 8, Table 2/Fig. 7 p. 21: FROG versus FROG (RND) aggregated method medians give AFP 0.69±0.13 versus 0.38±0.037, AF −0.33±0.14 versus −0.29±0.04, and AP 0.99±0.02 versus 0.64±0.03. Higher AFP/AP does not imply better AF in that comparison.

App. D.1, p. 20, Table 3: InforMARL solves all six single tasks at median fractions 0.994–1.000, versus 0–0.531 without an actor GNN; five-seed standard deviations are reported. This supports the chosen backbone's capacity within GRAFO.

App. D.2, pp. 20–21, Fig. 6: fixing encoder regularization to 10^10 while setting action regularization near 10^6 improves the EWC tradeoff; that diagnostic evaluates the whole TS sequence and is explicitly distinguished from first-two-task tuning. A strong nonfrozen baseline therefore depends on tuning budget.
App. D.4, p. 22, Fig. 8: the task-ID ablation removes the one-hot input; separate task-specific heads remain part of the reported task-incremental setup. It does not demonstrate unknown-task routing.

App. E.2–E.3, pp. 23–24, Fig. 9/Eqs. 13–15: explicit task graphs and orders are supplied; GFS encodes target edge distances. AF is average signed backward transfer, with higher/less negative values better, as confirmed by the negative axes in the rendered plots.

App. E.4, pp. 24–25, Table 4: hyperparameters include 5×10^6 environment steps per task, 50-step episodes, 32 parallel environments, 64 evaluation episodes and collisions disabled; tuning uses three seeds on the first two TS tasks. Links identify upstream JaxInforMARL and MEAL code, not a specified new GRAFO/FROG artifact.
llm_evaluation.rationale: A useful, in-scope contribution to general continual reinforcement learning: CGMARL formalizes graph-conditioned task changes, GRAFO separates topology, connectivity and feature shifts, and FROG freezes a first-task-trained graph encoder while regularizing the action module. Relevance is moderate because there is no language-model, tool-use or language-reasoning method. Ten-seed comparisons and ablations support broad empirical gains, but not uniform dominance: Figure 3 shows a lower TS AFP median for EWC (O) with FROG, and task order affects plasticity. Table 2 reports aggregated method medians of 0.69 versus 0.38 AFP for trained versus random frozen encoders, not a paired confidence interval. The theoretical argument is weaker than presented: Appendix A drops the assumed Lipschitz constant in Eq. 8, and the signed return-difference upper bound is not a bound on positive forgetting. Freezing removes encoder drift at a fixed input; it does not guarantee policy retention. Evidence is limited to small, collision-free formation tasks, one PPO/GNN backbone and short task-incremental sequences with separate heads; removing one-hot task IDs does not establish task-agnostic learning. Detailed task definitions, tuning and hyperparameters help reproducibility, but no new GRAFO/FROG release is identified in the supplied PDF, and no experiments were independently rerun. These are scientific and reproducibility limitations, not a material missing-source hold.

top5.summary: In Continual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CMARL), agents learn cooperative policies across sequences of tasks, aiming to adapt effectively to new tasks while preserving the ability to solve previously encountered ones. In many applications, tasks differ in their underlying structure, which can represent, for example, distinct operational conditions or target configurations (e.g., different network topologies in power grids or arrangements in formation control). Existing CMARL methods lack dedicated mechanisms to leverage this structural information when learning new tasks, failing to promote transfer and mitigate forgetting. To fill this gap, we propose Continual Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CGMARL), a novel framework for CMARL problems in which task sequences are mapped into a series of attributed graphs, each modeling a task-specific structure. In CGMARL, each graph determines the environment dynamics (next states and/or rewards) and the number of agents for the corresponding task. Then, we present Graph-based Formation (GRAFO), the first CGMARL benchmark, and show how forgetting arises in this setting. Finally, to address this limitation, we propose Frozen Graph Encoder (FROG), a method that relies on a frozen graph backbone to preserve past structural information in graph-based CMARL policies. Experiments on GRAFO show that pairing FROG with existing CL methods substantially improves performance on multiple CGMARL scenarios.
top5.summary_en: When a multi-agent reinforcement-learning system encounters a new formation or connectivity pattern, it must learn new actions without forgetting rules associated with earlier graph structures. This paper formalizes continual graph MARL with topology, connectivity and graph-feature changes, and introduces the GRAFO formation-navigation benchmark. FROG trains a graph encoder on the first task, then freezes it while the action module continues learning with regularizers such as EWC or MAS. Ten-seed experiments across three task sequences show improved final performance for many combinations, but not universal dominance. Table 2 aggregates method medians: average final performance is 0.69 with a trained-then-frozen encoder versus 0.38 with a randomly frozen encoder; this is not a paired confidence interval. Task order matters, and starting with easier tasks can reduce later plasticity. Freezing prevents encoder drift at a fixed input, but cannot guarantee that the overall policy will retain past skills; the appendix bound also omits a constant and misinterprets a signed return difference. Experiments use at most seven agents, disabled collisions, known task identities and separate heads, without real-network or language-agent validation. Its useful contribution is a framework for separately evaluating structural representation and decision adaptation, rather than a general solution to multi-agent forgetting.

top5.summary: In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.
top5.summary_en: The paper asks whether an agent forced to act before a deadline has enough observable information for a safe decision, even if its model is perfect. It represents the observation budget as a latency bound and assigns each true environmental state a set of safe actions. If two states produce identical observations before the deadline but have disjoint safe-action sets, no deterministic agent can guarantee safety in both. Start with the illustration on page 2 and definitions on page 3, then the signal-summation construction on page 4: two one-hot signals can sum to the same observation as one two-hot signal, permanently hiding source configurations that separate channels could distinguish. This establishes an existence example motivating joint design of safety specifications, sensing, environment assumptions and deadlines. It supplies no benchmark, measured success rate or large-language-model experiment. Important formal qualifications remain. Page 3 first requires a common safe action across the whole observational equivalence class, but then characterizes safety using pairwise conflicts. Three safe-action sets can overlap pairwise while their joint intersection is empty, so pairwise compatibility is insufficient for the general sufficiency claim. The infinite-state theorem also has order/diagonal-definition problems, and a finite action vocabulary does not imply finitely many conflicting states. These issues do not invalidate the elementary two-state example, but it cannot establish that every mixed-signal environment is unsafe. Use the paper as a design-review prompt: check observability, genuinely common fallback actions and formal assumptions before adopting a safety guarantee.

top5.summary: We propose a neural algorithm for sampling from distributions specified by unnormalized Boltzmann densities. Our approach is based on the Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto scheme for the Kullback--Leibler divergence in the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry (WFR JKO scheme). Our contributions are twofold. First, we prove that, for any fixed step size, the exact WFR JKO iterates converge exponentially fast to the target as the number of iterations tends to infinity. Notably, this result requires no structural assumptions on the target, such as log-concavity or a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Second, we develop a neural implementation of the WFR JKO scheme that parametrizes its transport and reaction components using reweighted normalizing flows. Numerical experiments on challenging multimodal targets demonstrate the promising performance of the proposed method.
top5.summary_en: This paper studies sampling from unnormalized Boltzmann densities, focusing on widely separated probability modes. Pure transport can struggle to cross low-density regions, while Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao geometry permits both transport and changes in mass. Reweighted normalizing flows represent these mechanisms, implicit JKO steps learn the density, and resampling followed by Metropolis–Hastings updates mitigates particle duplication. Read Theorem 3.5 in Section 3 before the implementation in Sections 4 and 5. Distinguish exact variational minimizers from finite-particle neural approximations: the target-independent geometric KL contraction guarantee concerns the former and does not directly cover training, numerical integration or resampling errors. Section 6 evaluates energy distance using seven synthetic distributions and 50,000 generated samples, reporting three best and four second-best results. However, on the hundred-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the error of 0.017 remains about 28.3 times that of importance-corrected neural JKO. Read the absolute values and sampling-error column in Table 2 rather than relying on ranks alone. The paper does not report across-seed uncertainty, compute-matched timings or rejuvenation-strategy ablations. Algorithms 2 and 3 in the appendix also contain inconsistent mass/log-mass and weight-normalization notation. These need checking before reproduction, but do not establish that the implementation producing the reported experiments used erroneous rules. The work offers methodological ideas for general neural sampling without directly validating benefits for language models or agents.

llm_evaluation.rationale: AttenFeed is a simple and potentially useful architectural probe: apply GELU to projected values and remove the separate FFN. Its generic token-level construction is a reusable Transformer-method contribution, so it remains in scope rather than being treated as a pure image-task application. However, all experiments are on Vision Transformers and language-model applicability remains explicitly future work; this limits relevance and generalizability. The strongest evidence is improved small-model image classification and matched-shape xViT ablations, not a proof that less inductive bias causes the gains. Parameter matching changes width, head count, depth and residual/normalization structure; no matched-compute or architecture-tuning comparison isolates the split. Appendix A establishes a conditional self-focused FFN reduction, but the claimed general attention equivalence contains unsupported assumptions and scaling errors. Cross-sample CLS effective rank does not directly measure within-image token collapse, and weight histograms are not functional-equivalence evidence. Transfer results are mixed, segmentation mIoU is worse throughout, seeds/error bars are absent, and training details contain an epoch inconsistency. Complete supplied-v1 text and material visuals are readable; these are scientific weaknesses, not missing-source grounds for a hold.

primary_link.title: On the Necessity of Attention-FFN Split in Vision Transformers

top5.summary: The standard Transformer architecture relies on a rigid pattern that alternates Attention and Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers. Despite its widespread adoption, the inductive bias imposed by this strict separation has not been systematically examined. In this work, we investigate the necessity of the Attention-FFN dichotomy in Vision Transformers (ViTs). To facilitate this analysis, we introduce the AttenFeed module, a unified component that integrates the functional properties of both Attention and FFN. Based on this module, we devise the unified Vision Transformer (uViT), which replaces the conventional alternating Attention-FFN structure with a sequence of AttenFeed modules. We then use uViT as a control group that relaxes the Attention-FFN dichotomy of the standard ViT and systematically compare the two models across multiple datasets and model scales. Our experiments reveal that the Attention-FFN dichotomy can hinder performance at smaller model scales due to the rigid parameter allocation of ViTs. The AttenFeed module and uViT serve as new analytical tools for understanding the Attention-FFN structure and offer theoretical insights into the heuristically designed architecture of conventional ViTs.
top5.summary_en: Must a Transformer alternate attention and feed-forward networks? AttenFeed probes this design by adding GELU to projected values, removing the separate FFN and stacking the resulting modules into uViT. To approach the baseline parameter budget, the authors also widen the models, change head counts and increase depth in the larger variant. Matched-shape small-model ablations support a classification benefit from the nonlinearity. On larger datasets, Small-model ImageNet accuracy rises from 53.64% to 67.11%, but gains shrink at Base scale and Large results are mixed. These comparisons do not isolate the attention–FFN split as the cause: width, residual structure and compute are not fully controlled. Transfer learning does not improve in every setting, while segmentation mIoU declines across both datasets and all three scales. Self-focused attention can reduce to a position-wise FFN, but the general attention-equivalence argument has assumption and scaling problems. Cross-image CLS effective rank is also not a direct measure of within-image token collapse. The paper lacks multi-seed uncertainty, contains an inconsistent epoch description and provides no language-model experiments. The practical takeaway is a simple architecture-ablation direction to test with matched compute, independently tuned recipes and repeated runs, rather than a universal architectural theorem inferred from small-model classification gains.

llm_evaluation.rationale: PairAudit contributes a general graph-conditioned error-prioritization and budgeted audit policy, so it is in scope as graph/ML methodology, but only peripherally relevant to the preferred language-model and agent topics. The useful combination is feature-gated Gaussian densities of frozen node/neighborhood predictions with paid pair audits and exact review-budget accounting. Four retrospectively chosen security shifts show positive mean net gains over uncertainty review across 36 fits, including all audit costs. This is simulated label revelation, not a human-review study; 600 pair-order runs per workload are not independent attack samples. primary_link.title: PairAudit: Guiding Human Review with Graph Tokens under Distribution Shift

top5.summary: Intrusion detectors can confidently misclassify attacks that were not seen during training. Human review can correct these errors, but only a limited number of cases can be checked. Uncertainty-based review may overlook confident errors, while anomaly scores alone do not show whether changing the review plan will correct more errors. We introduce PairAudit to find overlooked errors and improve review under a fixed budget. Its graph tokens capture prediction patterns across connected nodes. Rather than building another predictor through feature aggregation, PairAudit uses unusual relational patterns to uncover potential errors in existing predictions. Human feedback then helps decide whether these findings justify changing review priorities. Experiments across security tasks show that PairAudit corrects more errors on average than uncertainty-based review, including more errors on unseen attacks. These gains account for all review costs and do not require retraining the detector.
top5.summary_en: PairAudit asks how a fixed human-review budget can reach confident classification errors that uncertainty ranking overlooks. It combines a node's class probabilities with its neighbors' probabilities in numerical graph tokens, then uses feature-conditioned Gaussian-mixture densities to identify unexpected relationships. These tokens are not language-model text. The method proposes replacements for part of the uncertainty-ranked queue, samples candidate–original pairs, pays for both labels, and uses a Bayesian working model to decide whether to adopt the remaining replacements. Start with Figure 1 and Equation 4: both audited endpoints remain in the final review set, so auditing displaces other reviews. Then compare Tables 2–4. At a budget covering about ten percent of each pool, the four primary security tasks gain approximately 80–790 corrected errors over the uncertainty baseline after audit costs. Trust Score nevertheless corrects more errors overall on two tasks. The evaluation simulates noiseless label revelation; 600 audit-order repetitions are not 600 independent attacks or a human study. Neighborhood information helps unevenly, the working posterior is not a distribution-free safety guarantee, and even rejecting a proposal can incur a net loss because audit costs have already been paid. The paper is useful for error prioritization and review allocation. Operational use would still require checking reviewer time, labeling mistakes, and unequal consequences of different errors instead of assuming equal costs and equal correction value.
top5.summary_zh: PairAudit 探討固定人工審查預算下，如何找到分類器高信心卻判錯、因而被不確定性排序漏掉的案例。方法把節點與鄰居的類別機率轉成圖詞元，以特徵條件化的高斯混合密度辨識不尋常關係；這裡的詞元是數值向量，不是語言模型文字。它先提出替換審查名單，再隨機抽取「候選與原名單」配對、支付兩筆標註成本，用貝氏工作模型決定是否採用剩餘替換。閱讀時先看圖一及式四，理解抽查過的兩端都保留，且抽查會排擠其他審查名額，再看表二至四。四個主要資安任務在審查約一成資料的相同預算下，比原不確定性策略平均多修正約八十至七百九十個錯誤，已計入抽查成本；但 Trust Score 在其中兩項的總修正數較高。結果來自模擬揭露無雜訊資料標籤，六百次抽查順序重複並非六百次獨立攻擊或真人研究。鄰域資訊的收益因任務而異，工作後驗不構成無分布安全保證，拒絕替換也可能因已付成本而虧損。本文適合研究錯誤排序與審查資源分配；實際應用仍須檢查審查時間、標註錯誤和不同誤判代價，不能直接套用論文的等成本、等價值假設。
